props.title: Marathon Man

sections.content: Marathon Man revolutionized paranoid political thrillers with its brutal intensity and Laurence Olivier's chilling performance as Nazi dentist Christian Szell. Director John Schlesinger masterfully builds tension through the parallel stories of graduate student Babe (Dustin Hoffman) and his mysterious government agent brother Doc (Roy Scheider). The film's infamous dental torture scene remains one of cinema's most visceral moments, influencing countless psychological thrillers like Se7en (1995) and Oldboy (2003). Like Three Days of the Condor (1975) and The Conversation (1974), it tapped into post-Watergate paranoia while adding a personal revenge narrative.

sections.content: The film's genius lies in how it meshes real historical trauma with contemporary paranoia. Like The Boys from Brazil (1978) and The Odessa File (1974), it confronts the lingering specter of Nazi war criminals in the modern world. Hoffman's method acting approach - he actually ran marathons to prepare and stayed awake for days to achieve authentic exhaustion - set new standards for psychological thriller performances, influencing later intense character studies like Taxi Driver (1976) and Raging Bull (1980). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

Marathon Man created a template for thrillers where ordinary citizens face extraordinary danger, later seen in films like Enemy of the State (1998) and The Fugitive (1993). William Goldman's screenplay adaptation of his own novel demonstrates how to effectively translate literary suspense to screen, something later mastered in adaptations like The Silence of the Lambs (1991). The film's exploration of post-WWII Nazi hunting influenced everything from Apt Pupil (1998) to Munich (2005), while its dental torture scene became a cultural touchstone referenced in countless films and TV shows.
